newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's TMM says $280 mln payment ready.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's TMM says $280 mln payment ready.

text.p: Transportation company Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) said on Tuesday it is ready to pay the government some $280 million for its 40 percent share of the Northeast Railway concession.

The sum, due on Friday, represents the company's 40 percent stake in the railway line, a concession which TMM and Kansas City Southern Industries Inc. won last month with a bid of almost $1.4 billion.
"We've had the money in cash for a while now," TMM investor relations director Pedro Sanchez Mejorada said. "We will obviously need additional financing for the remainder due."
According to the government's financing scheme, the companies owe about $560 million on Friday and the remainder by June 5, six months after the company was granted the concession.
"TMM has a lot of cash -- about a half a billion (dollars) -- because its been building a war chest to bid on the railroad," Bear Stearns analyst Santiago Pique said.
Although Luis de Pablo, director of Mexico's state-owned railroad administrator, suggested recently the companies could make an advance payment, TMM spokesmen would not comment on the possibility.

TMM first held a majority 51-percent stake in the company formed for the bid, Transportacion Ferroviaria Mexicana (TFM). But TMM later sold a two percent stake to Grupo Servia, a holding company controlled by the same family that controls TMM.
The railway bid, considered surprisingly high, sparked concern among analysts, many of whom marred the companies' celebrations by lowering TMM's stock and credit ratings.

"The price is widely viewed as excessive for three reasons: estimates place the current book value of the railroad at no more than $500 million, the next highest bid was $541 million and the winning bid was not expected to pay more than $1 billion," Santander Investment's Jim Garvey wrote in a recent report.
TMM's shares in Mexico City have taken a beating since the announced railway venture, dropping from 51 pesos on the Dec. 5 bidding date, to Tuesday's price of roughly 34.6 pesos.
While many analysts agreed the 50-year operating concession is a good long-term strategic move, some said TMM's earnings would be diluted by the additional debt burden incurred.
"My concern is that in the near-term there is little upside potential, but I continue to like the longer-term prospects," Pique said.
TMM and Kansas City Southern hailed the purchase as the "NAFTA Railroad," an opportunity to secure trade channels from Canada to Chicago to Mexico City.

Transportacion Ferroviaria Mexicana (TFM), as the joint venture is called, plans capital investments of $227 million the first year of operations, $178 million the second year and $160 million the third year.
On Jan. 17, TMM entered a joint venture for Colombian ocean freight company called Transportacion Maritima Grancolombiana. The venture cost TMM only about $20 million, analysts said.
